Funny you mention this. The problem with small engines (and radiator sizing) is heat soak. The lion's share of a typical piston engine's heat loss is lost into the cylinder walls via a process called heat soak. This problem hits thrice, as energy lost to the walls is energy that is not creating pressure to drive the piston down, and further must be heat exchanged as a parasitic loss (on water cooled engines with pumps). Generally, because of cool boundary layer effects, the cylinder walls are kept relatively cool, but modern engines have larger cylinder 'squish', 'tumble' and 'roll' to aid fuel atomization, which erodes the boundary layer and drastically increases heat soak. So-called homogeneous charge engines have none of these losses as they don't need help atomizing fuel (via cylinder turbulence). The reason for the reduced fuel atomization performance? Ethanol. Although ethanol doesn't change the energy content of gasoline much, it drastically affects the aerosol mean droplet diameter.

This segues into your point about smaller engines. When you consider that heat soak is an engine's primary recoverable loss, and consider the surface-area to volume ratio of the cylinder, you will come to the conclusion that larger engines must lose less heat to the cylinder walls than a smaller engine would. This conclusion is, of course, correct. The most efficient engines always sport massive bores and strokes just for this purpose.

Also, for reasons I will gloss over (ask if curious), piston engines are always at their more efficient when run at WOT and max load, because of parasitic losses that don't vary much with load and other things. It's very counterintuitive (and rather uncomfortable), but the most efficient way you can operate the engine in your vehicle is like a switch - full throttle/idle. Caveat emptor for forced induction engines.
